In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of computing the degree of a node from its adjacency matrix.
the problem of determining the degree of a given vertex of an arbitrary directed graph.
the problem of determining the number of probes to the adjacency matrix of a graph required to find a specified vertex or edge of the graph.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the number of probes required for finding the degree of any vertex in a directed graph is at least ⌈n−1/2⌉+1 and at most 4n/3+1/6.
the number of probes to the adjacency matrix required to find a vertex of indegree k is exactly n−k+2k−1.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, for a directed graph with n vertices and m edges, we can compute the in-degree and out-degree of any vertex using O(n) probes to the adjacency matrix, or O(n+m) probes to the list adjacency matrix, or using O(n+log n) probes to the edge list representation, or using O(2 n−2 +n) probes to the incidence matrix.
we have found tight lower and upper bounds for finding a sink in an n vertex digraph from its adjacency matrix.
the number of probes to the adjacency matrix of an n-vertex graph to determine the degree of each vertex is 4n-⌈log n⌉-4 in the worst case, and 4n-2⌈log 2 n⌉+⌈log (n−1)⌉+3 in the average case.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in general, we cannot hope to improve the bounds for the adjacency matrix model by much.
the adjacency matrix of a graph can reveal a lot of information about its structure, and that this information can be extracted with a relatively small number of queries.
the adjacency matrix of a directed graph can be probed in order to learn about the degrees of the vertices of the graph.
